strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring social bias in masked language models and tracking changes after continued pretraining. The token-level prediction-quality scores offer interpretable diagnostics.

The experiments cover four public model checkpoints, two established benchmarks, multiple bias categories, and relevant likelihood-based baselines. Detailed category-level results expose substantial dependence on the model and dataset.
Retraining on stereotypical and anti-stereotypical sentence sets provides a useful directional sanity check. The proposed measures generally respond consistently to these interventions.
weaknesses: The human-agreement evidence does not establish the claimed superiority. Figure 3 reports best proposed AUROCs of 0.571 versus 0.569 for AUL on BERT, and 0.572 versus 0.566 on RoBERTa. These are small improvements with performance near chance, only 58 negative examples, and no confidence intervals or paired significance tests. The description of selecting thresholds to maximize AUC also needs clarification, since conventional ROC AUC integrates across thresholds.

The retraining evaluation appears to include the full CrowS-Pairs corpus after training on 80% of its sentences; no separate held-out bias results are reported. Consequently, improved prediction can reflect memorization and alignment with the training objective. The reported 100% accuracy concerns 72 aggregate model/category/training-condition decisions whose expected labels are inferred from the training corpus, rather than independently established bias outcomes. Evaluation on unseen pairs and balanced or neutral retraining controls would make this validation substantially stronger.

The interpretation exceeds the demonstrated construct validity. Human annotations establish whether the benchmark text expresses stereotypes, rather than the degree of bias in a model. Differences between metrics therefore do not establish that existing methods underestimate religious or disability bias. Such claims require an independent reference or should be narrowed to differences in measured sentence preference.

Several statistical conclusions are unsupported by the chosen tests. Section 4.2 applies unpaired Welch tests to matched sentence pairs and infers differences between models from differing significance outcomes, without directly testing the model contrast. In Section 4.3, McNemar’s test evaluates changes in binary preferences, whereas Equation 16 measures increases in continuous preference margins; significance for the former does not validate the latter. Uncertainty estimates and treatment of multiple comparisons are also missing.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed modifications. An all-token pseudo-log-likelihood baseline would help distinguish benefits of the scoring function from differences in which tokens are evaluated. Equation 10 changes both the rank transformation and attention weighting relative to CRR, so the existing comparison cannot attribute improvements specifically to attention.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the specified checkpoints, masking rate, epoch count, and split proportion. The manuscript lacks a code link, optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch size, seeds, exact split construction, and precise attention-aggregation details. Equations 1–2 also sum over all sentence tokens despite describing restricted target-token subsets, leaving baseline implementation uncertain. These reporting and validation gaps prevent a Findings recommendation, but appear addressable through a focused next-cycle revision.
